baslik: The Jet That Landed Safely — and Nobody Got Out
sonuc: landed after a cargo fire, but no one escaped
tetik: a fire in the aft cargo hold after take-off
mekanizma: cabin fire and smoke with evacuation never started after landing
ders: airlines stressed immediate evacuation after landing with a fire
yanilgi: The landing wasn't the failure. The aircraft stopped intact, but no evacuation began.
tartisma: Minutes passed on the runway with engines running. Who decides to open the doors?
basliklar: Why Nobody Escaped Saudia Flight 163
The Safe Landing That Became a Disaster
sahneler: An airliner caught fire soon after leaving Riyadh and turned back.
It landed safely, yet all three hundred one people aboard died.
Smoke came from a fire in the rear cargo hold.
The crew returned slowly and took time to stop.
After landing, the jet taxied off the runway.
The doors were never opened.
Smoke and fire filled the cabin before rescuers got in.
Airlines now stress immediate evacuation when fire is present.

baslik: Pilots Fixing a Navigation Fault Didn't Notice the Dive
sonuc: dove into the sea off Sulawesi
tetik: both pilots absorbed in troubleshooting a navigation unit
mekanizma: autopilot disengagement while the crew was distracted, leading to an unrecovered spiral dive
ders: Indonesia tightened maintenance oversight and crew training
yanilgi: The navigation fault didn't bring the jet down. Losing track of the aircraft's attitude did.
tartisma: The same fault had been written up many times. Why do recurring defects stay unfixed?
basliklar: Why Adam Air Flight 574 Crashed
The Navigation Fault That Distracted Both Pilots
sahneler: An airliner dove into the sea off Indonesia.
It broke apart at high speed, and all one hundred two aboard were killed.
A navigation unit had been faulty for weeks.
In flight, both pilots worked on it.
The autopilot disengaged.
The jet slowly rolled and nobody noticed.
When they did, it was in a steep spiral dive.
Indonesia tightened maintenance oversight and training.

baslik: The Pilot Fought the Autopilot — and Lost
sonuc: stalled and crashed on approach to Nagoya
tetik: an accidentally selected go-around mode
mekanizma: pilot pushing the nose down while the autopilot trimmed nose up, ending in a stall
ders: Airbus changed the autopilot so pilot inputs override it
yanilgi: The aircraft didn't fail mechanically. Pilot and autopilot were pushing in opposite directions.
tartisma: The software change was available before the crash. Should safety updates be mandatory?
basliklar: Why China Airlines Flight 140 Crashed
When a Pilot and an Autopilot Fought
sahneler: On approach to Nagoya, an Airbus pitched up steeply and stalled.
It crashed beside the runway, and two hundred sixty four people died.
The first officer had accidentally triggered go-around mode.
He pushed the nose down to keep landing.
The autopilot kept trimming the nose up.
The aircraft ended up badly out of trim.
When it pitched up, it stalled.
Airbus changed the autopilot so pilot inputs override it.

baslik: The Airliner That Nearly Landed on Four Other Jets
sonuc: lined up to land on an occupied taxiway
tetik: a closed parallel runway making the taxiway look like a runway
mekanizma: visual misidentification at night with one runway's lights turned off
ders: airports and aircraft added alerts for aircraft lined up on taxiways
yanilgi: No one crashed, but it was one of the closest calls in aviation history.
tartisma: There was no system to warn a crew lined up with a taxiway. How many near misses reach the news?
basliklar: How Air Canada 759 Nearly Landed on Four Jets
The Taxiway That Looked Like a Runway
soru: How many near misses go unseen?
sahneler: At night, an Airbus lined up to land on a crowded taxiway in San Francisco.
Suddenly the crew went around, passing just feet above waiting jets.
Four airliners were on that taxiway.
One runway was closed, and its lights were off.
The lit taxiway looked like the runway.
The crew asked the tower but didn't realize their mistake.
It was one of the closest calls in aviation history.
New alerts now warn when an aircraft lines up on a taxiway.

baslik: A Tired Crew Flew an Unstable Approach Into a Hill
sonuc: hit a hill short of the runway in Birmingham
tetik: an unstabilized, too-low night approach
mekanizma: continued unstable non-precision approach below minimums, compounded by fatigue
ders: cargo pilot rest rules were debated and approach monitoring was stressed
yanilgi: The aircraft was working normally. The crew continued an approach that should have been abandoned.
tartisma: Cargo pilots weren't covered by the same rest rules as passenger pilots. Should they be?
basliklar: Why UPS Flight 1354 Crashed
The Approach That Should Have Been Abandoned
sahneler: Before dawn, a UPS cargo jet crashed short of the runway in Birmingham.
It hit trees and a hill, and both pilots were killed.
The approach was flown at night without vertical guidance.
An autopilot mode wasn't set as intended.
The jet descended too steeply and too low.
Neither pilot called for a go-around.
Fatigue was found to be a factor.
Rest rules for cargo pilots came under renewed scrutiny.

baslik: Ice in the Fuel Starved Both Engines on Final Approach
sonuc: lost thrust on both engines on final approach
tetik: ice restricting fuel flow at a heat exchanger
mekanizma: ice crystals from the fuel accumulating and blocking the fuel-oil heat exchanger inlets
ders: Rolls-Royce redesigned the fuel-oil heat exchanger
zincir: VERY COLD FUEL ON LONG FLIGHT
yanilgi: The jet had plenty of fuel. Ice in the fuel blocked it from reaching the engines.
tartisma: The aircraft landed short, but everyone survived. How much is design margin worth?
basliklar: Why British Airways Flight 38 Lost Power
The Ice That Starved a 777's Engines
sahneler: On final approach to Heathrow, both engines of a Boeing 777 lost power.
Suddenly it dropped short and slammed onto the grass before the runway.
Everyone aboard survived.
The tanks had plenty of fuel.
On the long cold flight, ice had formed in the fuel.
When thrust increased, it built up at the heat exchangers.
The engines were starved of fuel.
Rolls-Royce redesigned the heat exchanger.

baslik: Two Pilots Took an Empty Jet to Its Ceiling for Fun
sonuc: crashed after both engines flamed out
tetik: the crew climbing to the jet's maximum altitude for fun
mekanizma: stall and engine flameout at 41,000 ft, then engine core lock preventing restart
ders: training on high-altitude operations and engine restarts was strengthened
yanilgi: The engines weren't defective. Once flamed out that high, their cores seized and couldn't be restarted.
tartisma: There were no passengers aboard. Does professionalism depend on who's watching?
basliklar: Why Pinnacle Airlines Flight 3701 Crashed
The Joyride to 41,000 Feet
sahneler: An empty regional jet crashed in Missouri after both engines stopped.
The two pilots were killed.
They were repositioning the jet with no passengers.
For fun, they climbed to its maximum altitude of forty one thousand feet.
The jet couldn't hold speed up there and stalled.
Both engines flamed out.
Their cores locked up and wouldn't restart.
Training on high-altitude flying and restarts was strengthened.

baslik: The Mid-Air Collision That Created the FAA
sonuc: brought down two airliners over the Grand Canyon
tetik: two airliners flying in uncontrolled airspace
mekanizma: collision in uncontrolled airspace relying on see-and-avoid among clouds
ders: Congress created the Federal Aviation Agency to control airspace
yanilgi: Neither crew broke the rules of the time. Outside controlled airways, avoiding traffic was up to the pilots' eyes.
tartisma: Air traffic control lagged behind the growth of air travel. How long should safety trail growth?
basliklar: The Grand Canyon Collision That Created the FAA
Why Two Airliners Collided Over the Canyon
sahneler: Two airliners collided over the Grand Canyon.
Both crashed into the canyon, and one hundred twenty eight people died.
They had left Los Angeles minutes apart.
Over the canyon, they flew in uncontrolled airspace.
Pilots were expected to see and avoid each other.
Clouds blocked their views as they converged.
It was the deadliest US air crash at the time.
Congress then created the Federal Aviation Agency.

baslik: The Take-Off With the Flaps Still Up
sonuc: crashed into a neighbourhood on take-off
tetik: flaps and slats not extended for take-off
mekanizma: take-off without flaps, missed checklist items and no effective take-off warning
ders: take-off checklist discipline and warning checks were emphasized
yanilgi: A take-off warning is meant to catch this. It either didn't sound or was not heard.
tartisma: The cockpit recorder captured casual conversation during checklists. How do you keep checklists sacred?
basliklar: Why Mandala Airlines Flight 091 Crashed
The Take-Off With the Flaps Up
soru: How do you protect a checklist?
sahneler: A Boeing 737 failed to climb after take-off in Medan.
It crashed into homes, killing people aboard and on the ground.
Its flaps had not been extended.
Without them, the wing couldn't produce enough lift at that speed.
The checklist item was missed.
The take-off warning didn't save them.
The cockpit recording showed casual talk during checks.
Checklist discipline and warning checks were emphasized afterward.

baslik: The Airship That Broke in Half During a Turn
sonuc: broke in two over the city of Hull
tetik: hard turns during speed trials
mekanizma: structural failure of a lightweight hull under aerodynamic loads from sharp manoeuvres
ders: airship design moved toward calculating aerodynamic loads
yanilgi: It wasn't a storm or fire at first. The frame itself buckled under loads from turning hard.
tartisma: The design saved weight to climb higher. How much strength can you trade for performance?
basliklar: Why the R38 Airship Broke in Half
The Airship Too Light for Its Own Turns
sahneler: A giant airship broke in half over the English city of Hull.
The wreck fell into the river and burst into flames, and forty four men died.
It was undergoing speed trials.
The crew made a series of sharp turns.
The hull had been built very light to fly high.
Its girders buckled under the turning loads.
The frame snapped, and hydrogen ignited.
Airship design then began calculating aerodynamic loads properly.

baslik: The Helium Airship Torn Apart by a Storm
sonuc: broke apart in a storm over Ohio
tetik: a violent updraft in a squall line
mekanizma: structural overload from storm-driven climb, with gas valves reduced to conserve helium
ders: later airships were designed for stronger structures and better weather avoidance
yanilgi: Helium didn't burn, so there was no fire. The ship was torn apart by the storm itself.
tartisma: The flight was partly a publicity tour. Should public relations ever set a flight schedule?
basliklar: Why USS Shenandoah Broke Apart
The Airship Torn Apart Over Ohio
sahneler: The US Navy airship Shenandoah was caught in a storm over Ohio.
It was torn into pieces, and fourteen men were killed.
Being filled with helium, it didn't catch fire.
A violent updraft carried it upward.
As it climbed, its gas cells expanded.
Some valves had been removed to save scarce helium.
The frame was overstressed and broke apart.
Later airships were built stronger and routed away from storms.

baslik: The Airship Crash That Made America Switch to Helium
sonuc: hit power lines and exploded
tetik: a rudder failure sending it toward the ground
mekanizma: loss of control leading to contact with high-voltage lines, igniting its hydrogen
ders: the US military stopped using hydrogen in airships
yanilgi: The rudder failure alone might have been survivable. Hydrogen turned contact with power lines into an inferno.
tartisma: Helium was scarce and expensive. When is the safer option worth the cost?
basliklar: Why the Airship Roma Exploded
The Crash That Ended Hydrogen Airships in America
soru: Is the safer option worth it?
sahneler: An army airship crashed into power lines in Norfolk, Virginia.
It exploded in flames, and thirty four men died.
Its rudder had failed.
The ship lost control and descended.
It struck high-voltage lines.
Sparks ignited its hydrogen.
It was the deadliest US airship accident at the time.
America then stopped filling its airships with hydrogen.

baslik: The Arctic Airship That Grew Too Heavy to Fly
sonuc: crashed on the Arctic pack ice
tetik: ice and weather making the ship heavy
mekanizma: loss of lift and control from ice accumulation and weather, with the envelope carried away after impact
ders: the rescue became one of the largest early international air-sea rescues
yanilgi: Not everyone died in the crash. Survivors lived on the ice for weeks in a red tent.
tartisma: Explorer Roald Amundsen died trying to help. How much risk should rescuers accept?
basliklar: Why the Airship Italia Crashed
The Red Tent on the Arctic Ice
hook: They lived in a red tent
sahneler: Returning from the North Pole, the airship Italia crashed onto the ice.
The impact killed one man and left survivors stranded.
The envelope drifted off with six more crew, who were never found.
Ice and headwinds had made the ship heavy.
It lost height and hit the pack ice.
Survivors camped for weeks in a red tent.
Roald Amundsen died flying to search for them.
It became one of the first large international air rescues.

baslik: Unlocking a Tail System Too Early Broke Up SpaceShipTwo
sonuc: broke apart during a powered test flight
tetik: the feather system unlocked early at high speed
mekanizma: aerodynamic loads deploying the tail feather after an early unlock, with no inhibit to prevent it
ders: an automatic inhibit was added to prevent early feather unlocking
yanilgi: The rocket motor didn't explode. A single early action let the tail fold up at high speed.
tartisma: The design had no guard against one human error. Should a single mistake ever be fatal?
basliklar: Why SpaceShipTwo Broke Apart
The Lever Pulled Too Early
sahneler: During a test flight, Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo broke apart.
Within seconds, it disintegrated, killing the co-pilot.
The pilot survived after being thrown clear.
Its tail feathered to slow it for re-entry.
The co-pilot unlocked that system too early, near the speed of sound.
Air loads forced the tail up on their own.
Nothing in the design prevented that single error.
An automatic lock was added to stop early unlocking.

baslik: The Jupiter Probe Whose Main Antenna Never Opened
sonuc: could not open its main antenna
tetik: ribs stuck after years of storage and transport
mekanizma: loss of lubricant on antenna rib pins, leaving several ribs stuck when it tried to unfurl
ders: the mission was saved by data compression through the small antenna
yanilgi: The mission wasn't lost. Engineers rewrote software to squeeze science through a tiny backup antenna.
tartisma: The delay after Challenger changed how the probe was handled. How do delays create new risks?
basliklar: Why Galileo's Antenna Never Opened
How Engineers Saved a Mission With a Tiny Antenna
sahneler: On its way to Jupiter, the Galileo probe tried to open its main antenna.
Suddenly it stuck partway open, crippling the data link.
The launch had been delayed for years.
The antenna was stored and shipped across the country.
Lubricant on some rib pins was lost.
When commanded to unfurl, those ribs stuck.
Engineers rewrote software to send compressed data through a tiny antenna.
The mission still returned groundbreaking science.

baslik: The Comet Probe That Broke Apart Leaving Earth
sonuc: broke apart during its rocket burn out of Earth orbit
tetik: the burn of its embedded solid rocket motor
mekanizma: likely structural heating from the solid motor's exhaust plume
ders: NASA stressed testing plume heating for embedded solid motors
yanilgi: Nobody saw it fail; the burn happened out of contact. Telescopes later spotted several pieces.
tartisma: The motor was fired with no telemetry link. Should critical events ever happen unobserved?
basliklar: Why the CONTOUR Probe Was Lost
The Probe That Broke Apart Out of Contact
sahneler: A NASA probe bound for comets fired its motor to leave Earth orbit.
Suddenly it went silent and was never heard from again.
The burn happened while it was out of contact.
Telescopes later spotted several fragments.
Its solid rocket motor was embedded in the spacecraft.
The most likely cause was heating from the motor's exhaust plume.
No one had watched the critical event.
NASA stressed testing plume heating for designs like this.

baslik: Russia's Mars Probe Fell Back to Earth
sonuc: re-entered the atmosphere instead of leaving for Mars
tetik: an upper-stage burn that did not happen as planned
mekanizma: failure of the second burn of the upper stage, leaving the probe in Earth orbit
ders: the loss set back Russian planetary exploration for years
yanilgi: The probe itself may have been fine. The stage meant to push it toward Mars didn't complete its burn.
tartisma: It carried small plutonium power sources that were never recovered. How should nuclear sources be handled on risky launches?
basliklar: Why the Mars 96 Probe Fell Back to Earth
The Burn That Never Happened
sahneler: Russia's Mars 96 probe was launched toward Mars.
Within a day, it fell back into Earth's atmosphere and was destroyed.
The rocket reached a temporary orbit.
A second burn should have sent the probe on its way.
That burn did not happen as planned.
The probe was left stranded and re-entered.
It carried small plutonium power sources, never recovered.
The loss set back Russian planetary science for years.

baslik: Sensors Installed Upside Down Crashed a Proton Rocket
sonuc: veered and crashed seconds after launch
tetik: angular velocity sensors mounted upside down
mekanizma: inverted rate sensors feeding reversed data to the guidance system
ders: Russia overhauled quality control at its rocket factories
yanilgi: The sensors had arrows showing the right orientation. They were forced in the wrong way anyway.
tartisma: The installer was a young technician; the checks didn't catch it. Who should catch a mistake like that?
basliklar: Why the Proton-M Crashed in 2013
The Sensors Hammered In Upside Down
sahneler: Seconds after lift-off, a Russian Proton rocket began to zigzag.
It turned over and exploded in a fireball near the pad.
Its angular velocity sensors had been installed upside down.
They were marked with arrows showing the right way.
They had been forced into place the wrong way.
The guidance system received reversed data and steered wrong.
No check caught the error before launch.
Russia overhauled quality control at its rocket factories.

baslik: A Power Glitch Reset a Rocket's Brain in Flight
sonuc: self-destructed shortly after launch
tetik: a momentary power interruption to the guidance computer
mekanizma: electrical short from damaged wiring resetting the guidance system in flight
ders: wiring inspection and handling rules for launch vehicles were tightened
yanilgi: The rocket's engines were fine. A brief power loss wiped its sense of direction.
tartisma: The payload was a costly national security satellite. How much redundancy is enough on critical launches?
basliklar: Why the 1998 Titan IV Launch Failed
The Power Glitch That Reset a Rocket
sahneler: Shortly after lift-off, a Titan IV rocket pitched over sharply.
It broke up and was destroyed, with its military satellite.
Its engines were working.
A short circuit briefly cut power to the guidance computer.
Investigators traced it to damaged wiring.
The computer reset and lost its reference.
The rocket turned the wrong way and triggered self-destruct.
Wiring inspection and handling rules were tightened.

baslik: The Liner That Sank in Fourteen Minutes
sonuc: sank in minutes after a collision in fog
tetik: a collier striking it amidships in fog
mekanizma: a large side breach with open portholes and too little time to close watertight doors
ders: the disaster reinforced rules on watertight doors and portholes
yanilgi: Unlike Titanic, there were enough lifeboats. The ship sank too fast to launch most of them.
tartisma: Open portholes let water flood in faster. Who is responsible for closing them at night?
basliklar: Why the Empress of Ireland Sank So Fast
The Liner Lost in Fourteen Minutes
sahneler: In fog on the St. Lawrence River, a collier rammed the liner Empress of Ireland.
In fourteen minutes, the liner rolled over and sank, and one thousand twelve people died.
Unlike Titanic, it carried enough lifeboats.
It sank too fast to launch most of them.
The collier had opened a huge hole in its side.
Water also poured in through open portholes.
Many passengers were asleep below.
The disaster reinforced rules on watertight doors and portholes.
